frontmatter.title: AI-Native Full-Stack Developer
frontmatter.subtitle: Interview & Role Revision Guide — PHP / JavaScript / Docker
frontmatter.author: Chris Garlick

blocks.content:
Focused revision for the **AI-Native Full-Stack Developer** role — a small, fast-moving, remote team where you build and maintain **PHP (8.x)** web apps while wiring in **LLM APIs, agents, and automation pipelines**. The role sits at the intersection of *software engineering, AI tooling, and creative problem-solving*. Salary **£45,000**, mid-level (2–5 yrs), reports to **Head of Technology / CTO**.

Each section opens with *why it matters for this role*, gives the concept in plain English, then a PHP/JS example or checklist you can speak to. The last pages give you likely interview questions and smart questions to ask **them**.

1. The Role, Mapped
2. PHP 8.x & OOP
3. Working with Legacy PHP
4. Design Patterns
5. A Major Framework (Laravel)
6. REST API Design
7. Auth: OAuth & JWT
8. Web Security
9. Databases (MySQL / PG)

10. LLM API Integration
11. Prompt Engineering
12. Loop Engineering & Agents
13. Model Orchestration
14. Coding Agents (Claude Code etc.)
15. Automation Pipelines
16. Webhooks & Idempotency

17. JavaScript / TypeScript
18. React & Vue
19. Docker & Containers
20. CI/CD (GitLab)
21. Cloud Deployment
22. Testing
23. Desirable: CMS & E-commerce
24. The Ideal Candidate
25. Interview Q&A
26. Questions to Ask Them

**How to use it:** read every *Why it matters* box, rehearse the *Say this* lines out loud, and be ready to tie each topic back to **real products you've shipped** — they explicitly want LLM integration in real products, *not just side projects*. Show AI is a core part of your toolkit, not an add-on.

This is **not a traditional backend role**. They want someone equally comfortable *prompting an LLM* and *writing PHP*. Map every requirement to a concrete thing you've built — specifics beat vague claims. They're lean and fast-moving, so signal that you **ship, own features end-to-end, and self-direct**.

rows: A PHP/Laravel app you built — models, migrations, services, tests.
A feature where you called OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini in production.
A workflow you automated — cron, queue, CI, or an agent loop.
A frontend you built that talks to your PHP backend.
An authenticated API you designed; how you handled tokens.
A GitLab/GitHub pipeline that deploys to Docker/cloud.
A Dockerfile / compose stack you wrote and shipped.
How you actually use agents day-to-day to move faster.

blocks.content: They value **curiosity about fast-moving AI tooling** and people who *proactively spot where to apply it*. Come with a recent example: a tool you tried last month, what you built with it, what you'd bring to their stack.

*"I treat the LLM as part of the stack — I'll prototype with an agent, wire the API into the product, then harden it with tests, retries, and cost controls. I like owning a feature from scoping to monitoring."*
The role asks for **strong, demonstrable PHP** including **OOP**. PHP 8 added real language power — be fluent in the modern syntax, not PHP 5 habits.

rows: Declare + assign properties in the constructor signature.
First-class enums (backed or pure) replace class constants.
Immutable once set — great for value objects / DTOs.
Skip optional params by name; self-documenting calls.
Strict (===) switch that returns a value; no fall-through.
Coroutine primitive; attributes power modern frameworks.

blocks.content: **Four OOP pillars, fast:** *Encapsulation* (hide state behind methods), *Abstraction* (interfaces / abstract classes), *Inheritance* (extend — but prefer composition), *Polymorphism* (same interface, different behaviour). Be ready to say **"I favour composition over inheritance and program to interfaces."**

This team has **legacy PHP, some still on PHP 5**. A real part of the job is *maintaining and modernising* it without breaking what works. **PHP 5 has been end-of-life since Dec 2018 / Jan 2019** — no security patches — so getting off it is both a quality and a **security** priority. Show you can be pragmatic: keep the lights on, then improve incrementally.

rows: Removed in PHP 7 — use PDO/mysqli with prepared statements.
PHP 7+ adds scalar, return, nullable & union types — add gradually.
Composer + PSR-4 autoloading; drop the require_once spaghetti.
PHP 7 turns many fatals into catchable \Error / \Throwable.
PHP 8 fixed string↔number juggling — old code may change behaviour.
Long gone — and a classic source of the app's old security holes.
Mixed HTML + PHP in one file
Separate concerns; move logic behind classes/services.
Add characterisation tests so you can change code without changing behaviour.
Go 5.6 → 7.4 → 8.x one hop at a time; get green before the next bump.
Rector applies mechanical upgrades; PHPCompatibility (phpcs) flags what breaks.
PHPStan / Psalm surface hidden type bugs the old runtime hid.
Route new features to new code; replace legacy piece by piece, not big-bang.
Isolate what you can't fix yet
Contain EOL code behind a WAF / network boundary; scan dependencies.

blocks.content: **Rector** (automated refactors/upgrades) · **PHPCompatibility** sniffs for phpcs · **PHPStan / Psalm** (static analysis) · **PHPUnit / Pest** (safety net) · **Composer** (autoloading & deps). An LLM/coding agent is genuinely useful here for grinding through repetitive migrations — a nice tie-in to the AI-native angle.

*"I'd stabilise the PHP 5 code with characterisation tests, then upgrade in small hops with Rector and PHPStan guarding each step — strangler-fig style, so new features go on modern code while I retire the legacy safely. Getting off an EOL runtime is a security win too."*
"Design patterns" is called out explicitly. You don't need all 23 GoF patterns — you need the handful you actually use and can explain *why*.

rows: Pass collaborators in, don't `new` them inside — testable, swappable.
Wrap data access behind an interface; swap DB/cache/API freely.
Pick an algorithm at runtime — e.g. choose which LLM provider to call.
Centralise object creation when construction is non-trivial.
Wrap a 3rd-party SDK (OpenAI/Anthropic) behind your own interface.
Add behaviour (caching, logging, retries) without touching the core.
React to something happening — dispatch events, run listeners.
One shared instance (used sparingly — DI container usually better).

blocks.content: **S**ingle responsibility · **O**pen/closed · **L**iskov substitution · **I**nterface segregation · **D**ependency inversion. The Adapter above is the *D* — depend on `LlmClient`, not a vendor SDK.
*"I wrap each LLM vendor behind one interface, so swapping OpenAI for Anthropic — or A/B-testing them — is a one-line change and every call site stays untouched."*

They want **a major framework**. Laravel and Symfony are the big two. Speak to whichever you know deeply — below is Laravel-flavoured, but the concepts (routing, ORM, DI container, migrations, queues) map to Symfony too.

rows: Map URLs → controllers; middleware for auth, rate-limit, CORS.
IoC container auto-resolves dependencies via type-hints.
Active-record models, relationships, eager loading (avoid N+1).
Validate input at the edge before it hits your logic.
Push slow work (LLM calls, emails) off the request cycle.
Decouple side-effects from the action that triggers them.

blocks.content: **N+1 killer:** `Article::with('author')->get()` eager-loads authors in 2 queries instead of N+1. Be ready to say you profile with **Laravel Telescope / Debugbar** and add DB indexes on foreign keys and frequently-filtered columns.
**Solid understanding of REST API design** is a named requirement — and everything AI-adjacent (LLM calls, webhooks, SaaS integrations) is API work.

rows: GET read · POST create · PUT/PATCH update · DELETE remove.
Each request self-contained; auth token on every call.
`/v1/…` or header — never break existing clients.
PUT/DELETE idempotent; use idempotency keys on POST.
One error shape: `{ error, status, details }`.

blocks.content: **422 vs 400:** use **422 Unprocessable Entity** for validation failures (well-formed but semantically wrong), **400** for malformed requests. **429** for rate limits with a `Retry-After` header. Knowing these distinctions signals real API experience.
The JD names **OAuth and JWT** directly. Know what each *is*, when to use it, and the failure modes.

**Delegated authorization** — lets a user grant your app scoped access to a *third-party* account without sharing their password. Flows: **Authorization Code + PKCE** (web/mobile apps), **Client Credentials** (server-to-server). You get an *access token* (+ refresh token). This is how you'd integrate a SaaS platform's API on a user's behalf.

A **JSON Web Token** — a signed, self-contained token: `header.payload.signature`, base64url-encoded. Stateless: the server verifies the signature instead of a DB session lookup. Store claims (`sub`, `exp`, `roles`) in the payload — **never secrets** (it's readable, only *tamper-proof*). Keep expiry short; use refresh tokens.

rows: Sessions = server state, easy revoke. JWT = stateless, scales, harder to revoke.
Short expiry + refresh tokens; or a denylist / token version claim.
Authentication = who you are. Authorization = what you may do.
Not quite — that's OpenID Connect (an identity layer on OAuth 2).

blocks.content: **Web security fundamentals** are required. Speak the OWASP language and show it's baked into how you build — plus the AI-specific risks, which will impress on this role.

rows: Prepared statements / parameterised queries — never string-concat SQL.
Escape output; CSP header; sanitise HTML; framework auto-escaping.
TLS everywhere; encrypt at rest; secrets in a vault, not code.
Allowlist outbound hosts — key when your server calls user-supplied URLs.
Treat LLM input/output as untrusted; sandbox tool calls; validate.
Never send secrets/PII to a model without need; redact & log usage.

blocks.content: **AI-native angle:** *prompt injection* is the new injection class — a malicious document can hijack your agent's instructions. Defences: separate system vs user content, least-privilege tool access, human-in-the-loop for destructive actions, and validate/parse model output before acting on it. Mentioning this unprompted shows you think about **AI security**, not just AI features.
**Manage relational databases (MySQL / PostgreSQL)** is a core responsibility. Know schema design, indexing, and how to diagnose a slow query.

rows: 3NF to avoid duplication; denormalise deliberately for read speed.
Index FKs + WHERE/ORDER-BY columns; composite indexes are ordered.
Read the query plan; watch for full table scans & filesorts.
Wrap multi-step writes; understand isolation levels & deadlocks.
PG: richer types (JSONB, arrays), stricter, CTEs; MySQL: ubiquitous, fast reads.
Version schema in code; make migrations reversible & zero-downtime.

blocks.content:
-- Diagnose before you optimise
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT a.id, a.title
FROM articles a
WHERE a.status = 'published'
ORDER BY a.published_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- Composite index that serves both the filter and the sort
CREATE INDEX idx_articles_status_published
    ON articles (status, published_at DESC);

**Postgres JSONB** is worth a mention on an AI role — great for storing variable-shape LLM output or embeddings metadata, and with **pgvector** you can do similarity search for RAG directly in Postgres.

The headline of the role: **Integrate LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini) into products and internal tooling.** They want *real production* integration — retries, cost control, streaming, structured output — not a demo.

rows: API key in env/vault; never in the client bundle.
Retry with exponential backoff on 429/5xx; timeouts.
Cache responses; pick the right model per task; cap max tokens.
Ask for JSON / use tool-calling; validate the schema.
Chunk & summarise; RAG for large corpora.
Log prompts, tokens, latency, cost per call.

blocks.content: **RAG in one line:** *embed your docs → store vectors → retrieve the top-k relevant chunks → stuff them into the prompt → the model answers grounded in your data.* Be ready to explain it — it's the most common production LLM pattern.
Listed under **Desirable Skills** (*prompt engineering methodologies*) and central to the AI-native philosophy. Show you have a *method*, not just vibes.

rows: Set a system role, then a specific, bounded task.
Show 2–3 input→output pairs to lock the format.
Ask the model to reason step-by-step for hard tasks.
Demand JSON / a schema; validate and retry on failure.
Fence user content so it can't be mistaken for instructions.
Give the facts in-context; tell it to only use those.
Build a test set; measure prompt changes, don't guess.

blocks.content: Vague asks · one giant mega-prompt · trusting output without validation · no evals · re-sending huge context every call (cache it) · putting instructions *after* untrusted user text.
*"I treat prompts like code — version-controlled, with a small eval set so I can measure whether a change actually improved accuracy before it ships."*
Named verbatim: **Build and maintain AI-powered workflows — loop engineering, agents, and model orchestration.** This is the frontier bit; being able to explain it plainly sets you apart.

**An agent** = an LLM in a loop with tools. It observes, decides, calls a tool, sees the result, and repeats until the task is done. **Loop engineering** is designing that loop well: what context goes in, when to stop, how to recover from errors, and how to keep it from running away.

rows: Max steps + a budget cap stop infinite loops and cost blowups.
Small, well-described, validated tools = fewer wrong calls.
Feed only what's relevant; summarise history as it grows.
Return tool errors to the model so it can retry/adapt.
Trace every step — prompt, tool call, result, cost.

blocks.content: Real systems use **more than one model / call**. Orchestration is routing work to the right model and chaining steps reliably.

rows: Cheap/fast model triages; escalate hard cases to a bigger model.
Break a task into steps; each step's output feeds the next.
Run independent sub-tasks concurrently, then merge.
A lead model plans and delegates to worker models/agents.
One model generates, another critiques and refines in a loop.
If provider A fails or is rate-limited, fail over to provider B.

blocks.content: **Cost/quality trade-off** is the real skill: default to the cheapest model that meets the bar, measure with evals, and only spend big-model tokens where it demonstrably helps. Frameworks worth naming: **LangChain**, **LlamaIndex**, and lightweight orchestration you roll yourself in PHP/Node when you want full control.
A specific responsibility: **work with and customize coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode.** They want daily-driver fluency plus the ability to *extend* these tools.

rows: A repo-level guide file steering the agent's conventions.
Reusable prompts & workflows for common team tasks.
Model Context Protocol — expose your tools/data to the agent.
Run linters/tests/format automatically on the agent's edits.
Delegate scoped tasks (review, search) to specialised agents.
Run agents headless in pipelines for reviews or fixes.

blocks.content: **MCP** (Model Context Protocol) is the key phrase to know — an open standard for connecting agents to external tools and data sources. Being able to say *"I'd expose our internal APIs to the agent via an MCP server so it can act on our own systems safely"* is exactly the customisation they're describing.
*"I use a coding agent daily — scaffolding, refactors, test generation — but I review every diff. I'll invest in a good project instruction file and hooks so the whole team gets consistent output."*
Don't oversell autonomy — they value *quality*. Frame agents as a force-multiplier you supervise, not a replacement for engineering judgement, tests, or review.

**Design and implement automation pipelines**, and **practical experience with at least one automation platform** is required. Show you can stitch systems together so work happens without a human clicking buttons.

rows: Webhook, cron/schedule, queue message, file drop, or event.
Decouple steps; retry failures; scale horizontally.
Safe to re-run a step without double side-effects (see §15).
Park poison messages; alert; replay after a fix.
n8n / Zapier / Make for glue; custom code for control.
Log each stage; alert on failure; track throughput.

blocks.content: **Concrete example to have ready:** *"A webhook fires → job lands on a queue → a worker calls an LLM to classify it → result written to the DB → a Slack/email notification goes out — with retries and a dead-letter queue for failures."* Name whatever platform you've actually used (n8n, Zapier, Make, GitLab CI, cron + queues) — one real one beats a list.

**Integrate SaaS platforms, third-party APIs, and webhooks** is a responsibility. Webhooks are how modern integrations stay real-time — and getting idempotency right is what separates a toy from production.

rows: Check the HMAC signature header against your shared secret.
Return 200 immediately; do the work on a queue.
Dedupe on the event ID — providers retry, so you'll see dupes.
Providers retry on non-2xx; make handlers safe to re-run.
Log raw payloads; support manual replay.

blocks.content: **Work with JavaScript / TypeScript** across the stack — you're *not siloed into backend*. Show comfort with modern JS and why TypeScript earns its keep.

rows: Non-blocking I/O; handle errors with try/catch; Promise.all for fan-out.
fetch(); read SSE streams for token-by-token LLM output.
Event loop, npm, building CLI tools & API servers.

blocks.content: **Why TypeScript:** *"Types catch a whole class of bugs at compile time, make refactors safe, and act as living documentation — especially valuable in a fast-moving codebase where the team is growing."*
**Frontend frameworks (React, Vue, or similar)** are named. You don't need to be a specialist in both — be strong in one and conversant in the shared concepts.

rows: React Query / SWR → Pinia + composables / TanStack Query.

blocks.content: **Key talking points:** component-driven UI, one-way data flow, the virtual DOM, avoiding unnecessary re-renders (keys, memoisation), and lifting state / a store (Redux, Zustand, Pinia) when it's shared. Tie it back: *"I've built the React/Vue front end that consumes the PHP API I wrote — so I own the feature across the stack."*

Docker is in the job title. Responsibilities: **set up deployment hosts using Docker** and **deploy/manage services in containerised environments**. Know images vs containers, Dockerfiles, compose, and good hygiene.

rows: Image = frozen blueprint; container = a running instance of it.
Recipe to build an image, layer by layer (cached).
Build in one stage, copy only artefacts to a slim final image.
Define multi-service stacks (app + db + redis) in one file.
Persist data / share host files into the container.
Services talk by name on a shared bridge network.
Config via env vars; secrets via secret stores, not the image.

blocks.content:
# Multi-stage: build deps with composer, run on a slim PHP-FPM image
FROM composer:2 AS vendor
WORKDIR /app
COPY composer.json composer.lock ./
RUN composer install --no-dev --no-scripts --optimize-autoloader

FROM php:8.3-fpm-alpine
RUN docker-php-ext-install pdo_mysql opcache
WORKDIR /var/www
COPY --from=vendor /app/vendor ./vendor
COPY . .
EXPOSE 9000
CMD ["php-fpm"]

**Good hygiene to mention:** small base images (Alpine/slim), `.dockerignore`, non-root user, pinned versions, healthchecks, and multi-stage builds to keep images lean. *"I keep the final image minimal and reproducible so deploys are fast and the attack surface is small."*

**Automate deployment using GitLab CI/CD pipelines** is a named DevOps responsibility, plus general **CI/CD and version control (Git)** experience. Know the pipeline anatomy and how a commit becomes a deploy.

rows: Pipeline runs stages in order; jobs in a stage run in parallel.
Pass build output between jobs; cache deps for speed.
Deploy targets (staging, production) with tracked deploys.
Masked CI/CD variables — never hard-code tokens.
`when: manual` to require a click before prod deploy.

blocks.content:
stages: [test, build, deploy]

test:
  stage: test
  image: php:8.3
  script:
    - composer install
    - ./vendor/bin/phpunit

build:
  stage: build
  script:
    - docker build -t registry.example.com/app:$CI_COMMIT_SHA .
    - docker push registry.example.com/app:$CI_COMMIT_SHA

deploy:prod:
  stage: deploy
  environment: production
  when: manual            # human gate before production
  script:
    - ./deploy.sh $CI_COMMIT_SHA

**Git fluency assumed:** branching strategy (trunk-based or GitFlow), meaningful commits, pull/merge requests with review, and resolving conflicts. CI = *catch problems on every push*; CD = *ship safely and often*.

**Deploy and manage services on cloud platforms** and **experience with cloud deployments** are required. You don't need to be a cloud architect — know the building blocks and how to reason about them.

rows: VMs, containers (ECS/Cloud Run), or serverless functions.
RDS / Cloud SQL — backups, failover, patching handled.
S3 / GCS for files, uploads, static assets, backups.
Distribute traffic; terminate HTTPS; health checks.
Store API keys/DB creds outside code & images.
Terraform / compose so infra is reproducible & reviewable.

blocks.content: **Frame it pragmatically for a startup:** *"I'd containerise the app, run it on a managed platform, use a managed Postgres/MySQL, keep secrets in a secrets manager, and wire logging + alerts. Reproducible infra over hand-configured servers."* Mention whichever cloud you've actually used (AWS, GCP, DigitalOcean, Fly.io, Hetzner).
**Write clean, testable, well-documented code and participate in code reviews.** They're *opinionated about quality but pragmatic* — show you know what to test and when to stop.

rows: One class/function in isolation; mock collaborators. (PHPUnit/Pest)
Real DB/queue; do the parts work together?
PHPStan/Psalm catch type errors before runtime.
PHP-CS-Fixer, ESLint, Prettier — consistent style, automated.
Mock the API; snapshot prompts; use evals for output quality.

blocks.content: **Testing non-deterministic AI** is a great thing to raise: *"I mock the LLM in unit tests for determinism, assert on the prompt I build and how I parse output, and keep a separate eval suite that scores real model responses against a graded dataset."* The **testing pyramid**: many fast unit tests, fewer integration, fewest E2E.
Under **Desirable Skills**: *headless CMS, e-commerce platforms*, plus *open-source contributions or a visible portfolio* and *AI agent frameworks*. Bonus points — mention any you've touched.

Content managed via API, decoupled from the front end. Names: **Strapi** (Node), **WordPress as headless / WPGraphQL**, **Contentful**, **Sanity**, **Directus**. Value: one content source feeds web, app, and AI pipelines.
PHP-heavy space: **Magento**, **WooCommerce**, **Shopify (APIs/apps)**, **Laravel + Stripe**. Talk to: carts, checkout, payment webhooks, idempotent order handling, PCI-safe token handling.

**AI agent frameworks** to be able to name: **LangChain / LangGraph**, **LlamaIndex**, **CrewAI**, **AutoGen**, plus **MCP** for tool integration (see §13). Even *"I've read the docs and prototyped with X"* shows the curiosity they want. **Portfolio:** have a GitHub link or a shipped project ready to point at.
Section 5 of the JD is pure culture-fit. In a lean startup, *how you think* matters as much as what you know. These are the exact traits they listed — mirror them with a story for each.

rows: AI as core toolkit, not add-on
A workflow where AI is embedded in how you build, daily.
A time you chose 'good enough to ship' over gold-plating.
A feature you took from idea to production, fast.
A time you clarified a vague brief before building.
Builds things that work at scale
Something you built that held up under real load.
A greenfield/uncertain project you drove forward.
Scoping → architecture → delivery → monitoring, all yours.

blocks.content: **Prep a STAR story** (Situation, Task, Action, Result) for at least three of these. They explicitly value people who *see the current AI moment as an opportunity, not a distraction* — let genuine enthusiasm show.

items: Walk me through a PHP feature you shipped end-to-end. Where did the tests and reviews add value?
How do you integrate an LLM into a production PHP app — auth, retries, cost, structured output?
Explain an agent loop. How do you stop it running away or costing too much?
What's prompt injection and how do you defend against it?
Session-based auth vs JWT — when would you pick each? How do you revoke a JWT?
You have a slow endpoint backed by a big MySQL table. How do you diagnose and fix it?
Design a webhook receiver that's safe under retries and duplicate deliveries.
Multi-stage Dockerfile — why, and what goes in each stage?
Describe a CI/CD pipeline from commit to production deploy.
How do you test code that calls a non-deterministic model?
Tell me about a time you shipped under ambiguity with an incomplete spec.
How do you decide when 'good enough' is good enough in a startup?
What's the most interesting thing you've built with AI recently?
How do you keep up with the fast-moving AI tooling landscape?
Describe a technical decision you made and how you'd defend it.

blocks.content: **Answer shape:** lead with the outcome, then how you got there, then what you'd do differently. Keep it concrete and tie it to *their* context — a small, fast-moving, AI-native team. Have numbers where you can (latency cut, cost saved, time-to-ship).
Good questions signal seniority and genuine interest — the JD explicitly values curiosity. Pick a few that fit the conversation.

- Where does AI already live in the product, and where do you *want* it next?
- Which LLM providers are you on, and how do you manage cost and reliability?
- Are you building agentic workflows in production today? What's worked / broken?
- How do you evaluate model output quality — any eval process yet?

- What does the stack look like today, and what's the biggest tech-debt pain?
- How do features get scoped and shipped — what's the path from idea to prod?
- What does success look like for this role in the first 3 and 6 months?
- How is the team using coding agents, and how do you keep quality high?

*"This role is exactly where I want to be — PHP fundamentals I'm strong on, plus building real AI features and automation. I like owning things end-to-end and I move fast without dropping quality. I'd love to help shape the engineering culture as the team grows."*

---

*Revision guide generated for the AI-Native Full-Stack Developer role (PHP / JavaScript / Docker). Good luck — go and show them AI is already part of how you build.*
